paras: The demands for the resignation of Black railway mail clerks were a series of notices that white residents along several Southern railroads served on Black postal clerks in early January 1903, ordering them to quit their runs. The earliest report said clerks on the Alabama and Vicksburg railroad in Mississippi were threatened with death, while later dispatches said no violence had been reported. Newspapers treated the demands as a spread of the dispute over the Indianola, Mississippi, post office, which President Roosevelt had closed after its Black postmistress resigned.

In the first days of January 1903, the president closed the post office at Indianola after the resignation of its Black postmistress, Mrs. Cox. The New Orleans States answered that if Roosevelt kept Black men in federal office, "his negro appointees will be killed." On January 5 the Post Office Department also learned that a posse at Boeuf River, Louisiana, had warned Charles Jackson, a Black mail carrier, not to return with the mail on pain of death.

A New Orleans special to the Houston Post, dated January 5, reported that whites along the Alabama and Vicksburg in Mississippi had told the Black postal clerks on that road to resign at once and "threatened them with death unless they comply." A Washington special to the Louisville Courier-Journal the next day described a milder step: three Black clerks on the same road had been "warned to ask the department for another route." By January 6 New Orleans dispatches said the demands had spread to the Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific, the Louisville and Nashville and the Southern Railway.

The New-York Tribune's correspondent wrote that the clerks were "in a condition bordering on a panic" but that no violence had been reported. No clerk or person issuing the demands was named in any report.

The protest from the Alabama and Vicksburg line was referred to Second Assistant Postmaster General Shellenberger, who said Southerners were "objecting to negro postal clerks" and counted at least two hundred on the Atlanta division. The Courier-Journal dispatch added that the president might discontinue all railway mail service in the South if the intimidation continued. No report of resignations, dismissals or route changes was found.

White papers carried the story for about a week, from the Houston Post's "Negro Clerks Warned" on January 6 to the Tribune's front-page "Rise Against Negroes" on January 7. The Courier-Journal's dispatch, reprinted in the Paducah Sun, called the demands "intimidation" and warned of "another bloody shirt crusade." Shorter versions ran in the Ocala Banner and in Louisiana's Lafayette Advertiser, which wrote that the administration faced "a grave problem."

In the Black press the Butte New Age reported on January 17 that a "general uprising against negro government employees" had occurred, naming the Queen & Crescent and the Louisville and Nashville. It placed the dispatch after the government's statement that the Indianola resignation had been forced by "a brutal and lawless element" on account of color. The Indianapolis Freeman covered the Boeuf River threat and the Indianola case but did not mention the clerks.

Accounts differ on what the clerks were told: a death threat in the Houston Post, a warning to change routes in the Courier-Journal, and a demand to resign with no violence in the Tribune. The railroads named also differ, and the figure of two hundred was Shellenberger's count of Black clerks on one division rather than a count of those warned.

reader.title: Demands for the resignation of Black railway mail clerks (1903)
bases: White residents along several Southern railroads demanded that Black railway postal clerks resign or change routes, in one report under threat of death; no violence was reported (A1, A4, A5).

No one was killed or attacked; the Houston Post reported a threat of death and the Tribune said no violence had been reported (A1, A5). The demands were aimed at the clerks' color and employment (A5).

Separate New Orleans and Washington dispatches to the Houston Post, the Courier-Journal and the New-York Tribune agree that whites along the Alabama and Vicksburg demanded or warned off Black mail clerks (A1, A4, A5); only A1 reports a death threat.

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'Rise Against Negroes' and the Houston Post's 'Negro Clerks Warned' reported the demands as a spreading consequence of the Indianola closing, with the Post Office Department's worry.
The Courier-Journal's 'Railway Mail Service May Be Discontinued' dispatch, reprinted by the Paducah Sun, framed it as 'intimidation' and feared 'another bloody shirt crusade'.
The Butte New Age placed the dispatch at the end of a column printing the government's statement that the Indianola resignation was forced by 'a brutal and lawless element'.
